title: Brute Force: Password Spraying
summary:
Password spraying is a credential access technique in which an adversary attempts a small number of commonly chosen passwords against a large number of accounts, inverting the traditional brute force pattern of many attempts against one account. The objective is to stay below per-account lockout thresholds and below anomaly thresholds that trigger on repeated failures for a single identity, while still finding the few accounts in any population that use a weak or seasonal password. Spraying is frequently directed at externally exposed authentication surfaces such as webmail, remote access portals, virtual desktop gateways, and identity provider endpoints, and it is often distributed across many source addresses to avoid source-based rate limits.

The distinguishing telemetry is a burst of failed authentications that is broad but shallow: many distinct usernames, few attempts each, a short time window, and a small set of repeated password-derived failure patterns. Domain controller and identity provider logs record the authentication package, the client address, the user agent or client string, and the exact failure reason, which separates a wrong password from a disabled account or a logon outside permitted hours. Successful authentication following the spray, particularly from a new address or an unusual client, is the pivot point that converts reconnaissance into an account compromise. Where multifactor authentication is enforced, the spray may still succeed against legacy protocols that do not support it, which is why protocol-level breakdown matters.

Legitimate causes of distributed failure bursts include stale credentials in a scheduled job, a misconfigured service account, or a user with an outdated cached password. The reliable discriminators are the ratio of distinct accounts to attempts, the synchronisation of retry timing, the absence of an interactive client fingerprint, and whether the source addresses belong to hosting or proxy ranges rather than corporate networks.
objectives: Explain why low-and-slow spraying evades per-account lockout thresholds and how distributed source addresses defeat source-based rate limiting.
Construct SIEM queries that surface broad shallow failure bursts and distinguish them from single-account noise.
Interpret authentication failure reasons and client fields to separate wrong-password events from policy or account-state events.
Identify which legacy or non-interactive authentication protocols bypass multifactor enforcement in a given environment.
Prioritise a spray investigation when a success occurs, and describe the immediate containment and reset sequence.
Map spraying behaviour to ATT&CK and mitigation coverage, and state where detection depends on external-facing service logging.
